## Sexual Mythology

Hardly anyone had real sex education. We learned from friends, from porn and by improvising, and what is left is a mythology: ideas everyone repeats and that are wrong. Here are 165 statements across twelve themes. For each one, you say whether it is a myth or the truth, and the explanation appears right away. The point of view is declared: sexual freedom, yes, and with responsibility. Without consent, without talking and without caring for whoever is with you, it is not freedom. There are two versions: the short one, with the 42 most important statements, takes about 14 minutes; the full one, with all 165, about 55 minutes.

- Getting things wrong here is no shame: it is the expected result of never having been taught. The test is for learning, not for grading a person.
- People are different: some more reserved, some more open, and both ways are legitimate. Nobody needs to be pressured into anything, and nobody needs to control what others do with their own bodies, as long as they harm no one.
- There are degrees of wrong. Sex without consent is violence; touching someone who does not want it is assault or harassment; insisting, pressuring and ignoring the other's pleasure is disrespect. None of these is the same thing, and all of them matter.
- Laws change from country to country. Check the law where you live.
- If any statement touches a hard experience, stop whenever you want. Seeking help is strength: the channels are on the Stay or Go page.

### Consent

What a yes is, and everything that is not.

- If the person did not say no, they consented. It is a myth. Silence is not a yes. Freezing and staying still are common reactions to fear. Consent is a clear yes, freely given.
- Someone who consented at the start can change their mind midway, and the other person has to stop. It is true. Consent can be withdrawn at any moment, and carrying on after that is violence.
- Someone who seduced, flirted all night or invited the other home and then changed their mind owes the other person something. It is a myth. Changing your mind is a right at any stage, and it creates no debt. The frustration of whoever heard the no is understandable; demanding, insisting or punishing is not.
- Starting foreplay and not wanting to go on to sex is a right. It is true. Each stage asks for its own yes. A kiss, a caress and undressing are not a promise of what comes next.
- When someone asks to stop in the middle of sex, it means the sex went wrong. It is a myth. It is consent working. Stopping at once, with no drama and no demands, is what lets the person feel safe to say yes again another day.
- Someone who is asleep, unconscious or too drunk to understand what is happening cannot consent. It is true. Without the ability to understand and decide there is no consent, even if the person does not resist.
- In a relationship or a marriage, sex is an obligation: there is no such thing as rape between partners. It is a myth. A relationship is not permanent consent. Sex forced by a partner is sexual violence, and the law of many countries recognises it.
- Agreeing to one thing (a kiss, going to someone's place, undressing) means agreeing to everything that follows. It is a myth. Consent is specific: it covers what was agreed to, and each new step asks for a new yes.
- Secretly removing the condom during sex is just a prank. It is a myth. The person consented to protected sex. Removing it in secret (stealthing) violates that consent and is already treated as a crime in several countries.
- Revealing clothes, flirting or a reputation for being easy work as an invitation. It is a myth. None of that is consent. The only invitation is the one the person makes, with clear words or gestures, for that thing and at that moment.
- Someone who consented yesterday has consented today. It is a myth. Consent does not accumulate. Each time is its own time, including in long relationships.
- Asking may I or do you want to ruins the mood. It is a myth. Asking is part of the game and can be said a thousand ways. What ruins the mood is carrying on with someone who did not want to.
- A yes given out of fear, after insistence or just to make the person stop asking is not consent. It is true. Consent has to be free. A yes that was extracted is obedience, not will.
- Sexual violence only exists when there is physical force. It is a myth. Threats, blackmail, abuse of authority and taking advantage of someone unable to decide are also sexual violence, even without a shove.
- Men can also be victims of sexual violence. It is true. They can, from any aggressor, and they tend to report less, out of shame and fear of not being taken seriously.
- An erection or lubrication proves the person wanted it. It is a myth. These are automatic body responses, which can happen without desire and even during violence. Researchers call it arousal non-concordance. Bodies do not consent; people do.

### Harassment and unwanted touching

What is done to the body and the space of someone who did not ask.

- Groping someone at a party, when they do not want it, is just fooling around. It is a myth. It is touching without consent, a crime in many countries, usually called sexual assault or sexual harassment.
- Rubbing up against someone on a crowded bus or train is a crime in many countries. It is true. It is a sexual act without consent, and many legal systems punish it with prison.
- Stealing a kiss is romantic. It is a myth. A kiss without consent is an imposed sexual act. Romantic is the kiss both wanted.
- Holding someone by the arm so they do not leave the conversation is just the persistence of someone interested. It is a myth. Holding by force is intimidation. Whoever wants to leave must be able to leave, without having to break free from anyone.
- Catcalling from a stranger in the street is a compliment, and the person should be grateful. It is a myth. For the person receiving it, it is usually embarrassment or fear, not a compliment. Nobody asked for a stranger's opinion on their body.
- Sending an intimate photo to someone who did not ask is a form of harassment. It is true. It is imposing sexual content on someone who did not consent to see it. Some countries already treat it as a crime.
- A boss or teacher who makes a job, a grade or a promotion depend on sexual favours commits sexual harassment. It is true. It is the use of power to obtain sex, and it is unlawful in most legal systems.
- Continuing to pursue someone after they said they are not interested is persistence, and persistence wins. It is a myth. After a no, insisting is disrespect. Repeated, it can become stalking, which is a crime in many countries.
- Comments about colleagues' bodies at work, even meant as compliments, can be harassment. It is true. At work nobody chose to be assessed by their body. What counts is the effect on whoever hears it, not the intention of whoever says it.
- Showing interest respectfully, once, and accepting the answer is not harassment. It is true. Flirting is legitimate. The difference lies in asking instead of imposing, and in accepting a no the first time. Where there is hierarchy, as between boss and employee, more care is needed.
- If the person laughed or looked awkward, they liked it. It is a myth. Laughing and looking awkward are common ways of protecting yourself in an uncomfortable situation. They are not a yes.
- Exposing your genitals or masturbating in front of someone who did not consent is violence, even without touching. It is true. Sexual violence does not require touch. Imposing a sexual act on someone's sight is a crime in many countries.

### Pressure, insistence and doubt

The zone where there was no force, and still it was not free.

- If the person hesitates about coming up to your place, the right thing is to insist until they make up their mind. It is a myth. Doubt is not a yes. The right thing is not to insist and to leave the door open: whoever wants to will come back.
- Insisting until the person gives in is a form of coercion, even without a threat. It is true. Wearing someone down produces a yes that is not free. Research calls it verbal sexual coercion.
- If you loved me, you would is a fair argument. It is a myth. It is emotional blackmail: it uses love as currency. Loving someone obliges nobody to any practice.
- Sulking, giving the silent treatment or making the person feel guilty after a no is a form of pressure. It is true. It punishes the no. Someone who learns that refusing is costly starts saying yes out of fear.
- Giving someone drinks to make them easier is seduction. It is a myth. It is deliberately taking away the ability to decide. Sex with someone unable to consent is violence.
- Whoever paid for dinner has the right to expect something in return. It is a myth. Kindness is not a down payment. Nobody owes sex for dinner, a gift, a lift or a place to stay.
- Once started, a man can no longer stop. It is a myth. He can. Stopping may be frustrating, but it is always possible, and it is an obligation when the other asks.
- A maybe or a not now should be treated as a no, for the time being. It is true. Only a clear yes authorises. Maybe means a conversation or waiting, never go ahead.
- Threatening to break up if the person does not accept a practice is negotiating. It is a myth. Saying that a difference matters to you is honest. Using the threat to extract a yes is coercion.
- Being very aroused without reaching orgasm is bad for your health. It is a myth. It can cause a passing discomfort, which is harmless and goes away on its own. It is not an illness and creates no debt for anyone.
- Saying no to someone you love, without giving a reason, is a right. It is true. Nobody has to justify a no. Explaining may help the relationship, but it is not a condition for the no to count.
- Agreeing on one thing and doing another during sex, without asking, breaks consent. It is true. The yes was for what was agreed. Switching practice without asking is deciding alone about the other's body.

### Pleasure and the porn script

What the screen taught and what a real body asks for.

- Sex in porn shows what sex is usually like. It is a myth. Porn is staged: actors, cuts, angles and a script. It does not show the talking, the lubricant, the condom, the pause or what went wrong.
- Watching porn compulsively, unable to stop even when it gets in the way of life, is a health problem that deserves help. It is true. The World Health Organization recognises compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, a diagnosis also used for out-of-control pornography use: months of lost control, with distress or impairment in life. Specialists still debate whether addiction is the right word, and the WHO did not classify it that way; that it does harm and can be treated, nobody disputes.
- Someone who watches porn now and then is already addicted. It is a myth. What defines the problem is loss of control and impairment in life, not frequency. Feeling guilty because you disapprove of porn is not, on its own, a sign of a disorder.
- Most women reach orgasm from penetration alone. It is a myth. In an American survey of more than a thousand women, published in 2018, about one in five said penetration alone was enough. For nearly three in four, clitoral stimulation is necessary or makes orgasm better.
- The clitoris is much bigger than the part you can see. It is true. The visible part is only the tip. The organ continues inside, for several centimetres, around the vaginal opening.
- Sex ends when the man comes. It is a myth. That is the porn script, not a rule. Sex ends when both want it to, and one person's pleasure does not close the other's.
- In sex between a man and a woman, women have orgasms less often than men. It is true. It is the so-called orgasm gap, measured in large surveys. It is much smaller when there is oral sex, clitoral stimulation and talking, which points to the script, not the body.
- Faking orgasm helps the relationship. It is a myth. Faking teaches your partner to repeat exactly what does not work. Saying what works is harder, and it solves the problem.
- Using lubricant is a sign that something is wrong. It is a myth. Lubrication varies with the cycle, age, medication and tiredness. Lubricant adds comfort and pleasure, and protects the condom from tearing.
- Good sex is sex that lasts a long time. It is a myth. In a small survey of sex therapists in the United States and Canada, 3 to 13 minutes of penetration were rated adequate or desirable. Duration does not measure pleasure.
- Penis size is what matters most for the other person's pleasure. It is a myth. Attention, rhythm, stimulation in the right place and talking matter far more. Worrying about size is one more effect of porn.
- Looking after only your own pleasure and ignoring the other's is a selfish way of having sex, even with consent. It is true. Consent is the minimum, not the goal. Sex between two people in which only one matters treats the other as a tool.
- Practices common in porn, such as choking, slapping or coming on the face, can be done without asking, because everyone expects them. It is a myth. No practice does away with agreement. And pressure on the neck carries serious risk even without leaving a mark: there is no guaranteed safe way to do it.
- You can have great sex without penetration. It is true. Sex is far more than penetration. For many people, and in many bodies, the best of it is in the rest.
- Masturbation is bad for your health. It is a myth. It is not. It is a safe way of knowing your own body, at any adult age and with or without a partner.
- Losing an erection or not having an orgasm now and then is common and does not mean lack of desire. It is true. Tiredness, anxiety, alcohol and distraction are enough for that. It becomes a medical matter only when it is frequent and bothers you.
- Pain during sex is normal, especially for women. It is a myth. Pain is a signal to stop. Usually arousal, time or lubricant is missing; if it persists, it calls for a consultation, not for putting up with it.
- The first time always hurts and always bleeds. It is a myth. Many people feel no pain and do not bleed. Calm, arousal and lubrication make more difference than any myth about the hymen.

### Body, desire and self-discovery

How the body works, without the legends, and why yours is worth knowing.

- Exploring your own body is for people who do not have a partner. It is a myth. Knowing your own body is for everyone, with or without a partner. Whoever knows what they like can show the other.
- Knowing your own body by yourself helps you have pleasure with someone else. It is true. Where, how and at what rhythm your body responds is information no partner can guess.
- Looking closely at your own genitals, with a mirror if needed, is a healthy way of knowing yourself. It is true. Many people have never looked. Knowing your own anatomy helps with pleasure and with noticing early when something changes.
- You can tell whether a woman is a virgin by examining the hymen. It is a myth. You cannot. The World Health Organization states that so-called virginity testing has no scientific basis and violates human rights.
- The vagina becomes permanently loose in someone who has had many partners. It is a myth. The vagina is an elastic muscular canal that returns to its resting state. The number of partners changes nobody's anatomy.
- Men always have more desire than women. It is a myth. On average, studies find more desire reported by men, but the variation between people is huge. In many couples it is the woman who wants more.
- Desire can appear out of nowhere or only after stimulation, and both ways are normal. It is true. These are spontaneous desire and responsive desire. Someone who only feels like it once the touching starts has no defect at all.
- A natural smell, discharge and hair on the vulva are signs of poor hygiene. It is a myth. They are features of a healthy body. The vagina cleans itself, and douching is linked to more infections.
- People with disabilities do not have a sex life. It is a myth. They have desire, a sex life and the right to sex education like anyone else, and disability does not, in itself, take away the capacity to consent. The rule for everyone applies: someone who is not able to understand and decide about the act cannot consent, and sex with that person is violence. This is assessed case by case, not by the diagnosis.
- After a certain age, sex is over. It is a myth. It changes, but it does not end. Many people keep an active sex life after 60 and after 70.
- Erection difficulties and premature ejaculation are common and treatable. It is true. They are among the most frequent sexual complaints among men. They are treatable, and the shame of talking is the biggest obstacle.
- Sexual orientation can be changed with therapy. It is a myth. So-called conversion therapies do not work and cause harm. They are condemned by the major health bodies, and banned in a growing number of countries.

### Different bodies, perfect body

Sizes, colours, shapes, hair and the pressure to fix what is not broken.

- There is one normal shape for genitals, and anyone outside it has a problem. It is a myth. Vulvas, clitorises, penises, breasts, nipples and anuses vary a great deal in size, colour and shape. What appears in porn is a selected sample, often surgically altered, not the standard. The Labia Library, run by an Australian women's health organisation, shows that variety in real, unretouched photos. [Labia Library](https://www.labialibrary.org.au/)
- One breast bigger than the other, inner lips that show on the outside and a slightly curved penis are common variations. It is true. Asymmetry is the rule, not the exception. See a doctor when there is pain, a sudden change or a curve that gets in the way.
- The skin of the genitals and the anus is usually darker than the rest of the body, and that is normal. It is true. It happens in every skin tone, as an effect of hormones. Intimate bleaching is a cosmetic procedure, not a health need.
- Penises and vulvas are body parts like any other: they call for neither worship nor shame. It is true. Treating genitals as a trophy or as a taboo gives them a weight that gets in the way: performance anxiety on one side and shame on the other. They are ordinary parts of the body, and everyone has theirs.
- Removing pubic hair is more hygienic. It is a myth. There is no medical or hygienic reason to remove the hair, and removal can irritate, cause ingrown hairs and injure the skin. Keeping it, trimming it or removing it is up to whoever owns the body.
- Someone with a preference can demand that their partner remove their body hair, or stop removing it. It is a myth. A preference is stated; a demand over someone else's body is control. The decision belongs to whoever lives in that body.
- According to a review of studies published in 2015, the average erect penis is around 13 centimetres. It is true. The review pooled measurements of up to 15,000 men, taken by professionals; the erect measurement came from a smaller group of about 700. Most men who think they are small are within the average.
- There are pills, creams and devices that are proven to enlarge the penis. It is a myth. No product has demonstrated efficacy. And the American Urological Association states that cosmetic enlargement surgeries, such as fat injection and cutting the ligament, have not been shown to be safe or effective.
- The bodies in porn and on social media are ordinary bodies. It is a myth. They are selected bodies, often operated on, hairless, lit and edited. Comparing yours with them is comparing real life with a shop window.
- Cosmetic surgery on the genitals carries risks, and good-quality data that it works is lacking. It is true. Pain, bleeding, infection and scarring are among the complications. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists advises that the person be told this before deciding.
- Getting implants, having intimate surgery or changing nothing is each person's decision; pressuring someone to change their body is disrespect. It is true. It works both ways: nobody should be pushed into surgery or judged for having had it. The problem is the pressure, not the choice.
- Some people are born with sex characteristics that do not fit the typical definitions of male or female. It is true. They are intersex people: the variation can be in the chromosomes, the hormones, the gonads or the genitals. The UN estimates that they are between 0.05% and 1.7% of the population.
- Intersex people have both sets of genitals, complete. It is a myth. That does not happen in humans. This is why the term hermaphrodite, which is inaccurate, has fallen out of use, and many people consider it offensive. What exists are variations, many of them invisible from the outside.

### Prevention: pregnancy and STIs

What protects, what does not, and what hardly anyone tells you.

- Pulling out before coming is a safe way to avoid pregnancy. It is a myth. In typical use, about one in five people relying on it alone gets pregnant within a year. And it protects against no STI.
- The fluid that comes out before ejaculation can cause pregnancy. It is true. It can contain sperm. It is one of the reasons withdrawal fails so often.
- You can get pregnant from sex during a period. It is true. It is less likely, but possible: sperm survive for several days, and ovulation can come early.
- You can have an STI and feel nothing. It is true. Chlamydia, HPV, HIV and others can go months or years without symptoms. That is why testing matters more than appearance.
- Oral sex does not transmit STIs. It is a myth. It transmits herpes, gonorrhoea, syphilis and HPV, among others. Condoms and barriers apply to oral sex too.
- Condoms protect against pregnancy and most STIs, but not all of them equally. It is true. They greatly reduce the risk of HIV, gonorrhoea and chlamydia. HPV and herpes also pass through skin the condom does not cover.
- The contraceptive pill protects against STIs. It is a myth. The pill only prevents pregnancy. Against STIs, what protects is the condom.
- Any lubricant can be used with a condom. It is a myth. Oil-based lubricants, such as petroleum jelly and massage oil, weaken latex. With a condom, use water-based or silicone-based ones.
- A person with HIV who is on treatment and has an undetectable viral load does not transmit the virus through sex. It is true. It is the consensus known as undetectable equals untransmittable, backed by large studies and adopted by the World Health Organization and UNAIDS.
- There are medicines that prevent HIV infection, before and after exposure. It is true. PrEP is taken before; PEP, after, and it has to start within 72 hours. Ask a health service where to get them in your country.
- The morning-after pill causes an abortion. It is a myth. It works by delaying ovulation. According to the World Health Organization, it does not interrupt a pregnancy that has already begun.
- There is a vaccine against HPV, and it is for any gender. It is true. The vaccine prevents the main HPV types linked to genital warts and to cancers of the cervix, penis, anus and throat.
- Only people with many partners get STIs. It is a myth. One unprotected encounter with one person who has the infection, often without knowing, is enough.
- Getting tested for STIs from time to time and telling your partner the result is part of having sex responsibly. It is true. Up-to-date tests and a frank conversation protect both. Having an STI is no shame; hiding it is what takes away the other's chance to choose.
- You can tell from appearance whether someone has an STI. It is a myth. You cannot. Most infections do not show on the body, and healthy, good-looking people transmit them like anyone else.
- Washing or urinating after sex prevents pregnancy and STIs. It is a myth. It prevents neither. Urinating afterwards may, at most, help prevent a urinary infection.

### Judgement and prejudice

What morality repeats and science does not support.

- Being a virgin after 25 or 30 is a sign that something is wrong with the person. It is a myth. There is no right age. Some start early, late or never, by choice, circumstance or orientation, and none of that is a defect.
- Virginity is a social idea, not a medical fact. It is true. There is no test that proves it and no single definition: each culture decides what counts as the first time.
- Someone who has had many partners is worth less as a person or as a partner. It is a myth. The number of partners measures neither character nor the capacity to love or be faithful. What measures it is how the person treats whoever is with them.
- Having a fetish lived with consent and without harming anyone is not an illness. It is true. Current medical classifications only speak of a disorder when there is distress or impairment for the person, serious risk of injury or involvement of someone who did not consent.
- A man who likes being penetrated is gay. It is a myth. A practice does not define orientation. Orientation is about who the person is attracted to, not what they like to do.
- Bisexual people are undecided or going through a phase. It is a myth. Bisexuality is a stable orientation, recognised by research. It is not a stage on the way to something else.
- A woman who takes the initiative or likes casual sex has no self-respect. It is a myth. It is the double standard: the same behaviour praised in a man becomes grounds for judging a woman.
- A man who turns down sex has some problem. It is a myth. Men also have days without desire, limits and the right to say no. Desire is no gender's obligation.
- Homosexuality is not an illness: the World Health Organization removed it from its list of diseases in 1990. It is true. The decision dates from 17 May 1990, the date that became the international day against homophobia.
- Someone with no interest in sex needs treatment. It is a myth. Asexuality is an orientation. Seeking help only makes sense when the lack of desire is a change that bothers the person themselves.
- Telling friends intimate details about someone, or spreading who they have been with, is a form of disrespect. It is true. The intimacy was shared with you, not with your group. Exposing the other breaks the trust that made it possible.
- Someone who likes porn, toys or masturbating while in a relationship does so because their partner is not enough. It is a myth. Pleasure alone and pleasure together do not compete. It becomes a problem when it is hidden against an agreement or when it replaces the encounter.
- Someone who is reserved, wants little or prefers simple sex is repressed and needs to loosen up. It is a myth. People are different: some more reserved, some more open. Neither way is a defect, and nobody should be pushed towards the other.
- What adults do with their own bodies, with consent and without harming anyone, is not for others to control. It is true. You may not want it for yourself, and that is a legitimate limit. Wanting to forbid or shame the other is already control.
- You can keep an open mind about other people's choices without wanting the same things for yourself. It is true. Respecting is not taking part. You can keep your limits and, at the same time, not judge those who live differently without harming anyone.
- Sexual freedom means being up for everything. It is a myth. Freedom includes the no. Someone who feels obliged to be up for everything in order to be modern has swapped one rule for another.
- Sexual freedom and responsibility go together. It is true. Being able to choose includes caring for whoever is with you: telling the truth, protecting both people's health and respecting the no.

### Agreements and cheating

What was agreed, spoken or not, and what happens when someone breaks it.

- Being with someone else in a relationship that does not allow it breaks the agreement, even if it meant nothing. It is true. The agreement was about the act, not the feeling. What weighs on the person cheated on is the breach and the lie.
- If your partner never finds out, nobody was harmed. It is a myth. They were: it took away their chance to decide about their own life with the true information, and may have put their health at risk.
- An open relationship is cheating by another name. It is a myth. The difference is the informed consent of everyone involved. Cheating is what is done in secret against the agreement.
- In an open relationship anything goes. It is a myth. An open relationship has rules, often more explicit than those of monogamy. Breaking them is also cheating.
- What counts as cheating is the same for everyone. It is a myth. Each person draws the line somewhere: for some it is the kiss, for others the hidden conversation. That is why rules have to be spoken, not presumed.
- Having unprotected sex with someone else and then with your partner, without telling them, puts their health at risk without their being able to choose. It is true. Beyond the breach of agreement, it is a decision about the other's body taken without them.
- The person who was cheated on is to blame, for not giving enough attention. It is a myth. Dissatisfaction may explain the wish. The choice to lie instead of talking or ending it belongs to whoever lied.
- Feeling attracted to someone else now and then means love is over. It is a myth. Feeling attraction to others is common in any relationship. What counts is what you do with it, and whether that respects the agreement.
- Proposing to open the relationship is legitimate; pressuring after a no is coercion. It is true. Proposing is putting a wish on the table. Insisting, punishing or threatening until the other gives in turns the agreement into an imposition.
- Jealousy is proof of love. It is a myth. Jealousy is a common emotion, which comes from fear of loss or from the idea of possession. Watching, forbidding and isolating are not love: they are control, and they are warning signs.
- Controlling your partner's clothes, friendships or sexual past is a form of care. It is a myth. It is control. Caring is wanting the other's good; controlling is deciding for them what they may do with their own body and life.
- Checking your partner's phone in secret is a right of those who love. It is a myth. It is a violation of privacy and a sign that trust is already broken. The way out is a conversation, not surveillance.
- Lying about being single, about using protection or about having an STI in order to get sex takes informed consent away from the other. It is true. The person said yes to a situation that was not the real one. In some countries, lies like these have legal consequences.

### Conversation and emotional intelligence

What is said before, during and after.

- When there is love, the other knows what I like without my having to say it. It is a myth. Nobody reads minds. Expecting guesswork is the shortest road to frustration for both.
- Couples who talk about sex outside the bedroom tend to have more sexual satisfaction. It is true. A 2022 review pooling 93 studies found this association: talking about what you like and do not like goes together with more sexual and relationship satisfaction.
- Saying I don't like that during sex is offensive and should be avoided. It is a myth. It is the most useful information anyone can receive. It can be said kindly, and preferably along with what you do like.
- Asking afterwards whether it was good and whether anything bothered them is care, not insecurity. It is true. The question opens room for what the person did not have the courage to say at the time.
- Seeing the other only as a means of getting pleasure, without caring what they feel, is objectifying. It is true. Objectifying is treating a person as a thing: using the body and ignoring the will, the pleasure and the feelings of whoever is there.
- Feeling desire for someone's body is already objectifying them. It is a myth. Desiring someone's body is part of attraction. It becomes objectification when the body is all you see and the person stops counting.
- In casual sex there is no need to care about what the other feels. It is a myth. Casual means without commitment, not without consideration. On the other side there is still a person, with feelings and limits.
- Casual sex does away with honesty about what each one wants. It is a myth. Sex without commitment is legitimate. Letting the other believe something you do not intend is a lack of emotional responsibility.
- Promising a relationship or saying I love you just to get sex is manipulation. It is true. The other's consent was given on the basis of a lie. It is using someone's feelings as a tool.
- Someone with a lot of experience does not need to ask: they know what the other wants. It is a myth. Every person is a different body and a different story. Real experience is knowing that you need to ask.
- Feeling ashamed to talk about sex is common, and it can be learned. It is true. Hardly anyone was taught to have this conversation. It improves with practice, like any other.
- Agreeing beforehand on the condom, the limits and a safe word takes away spontaneity. It is a myth. Agreeing is what allows you to let go: whoever knows where the limits are can relax within them.
- Noticing the other's body (tension, silence, going still) and stopping to ask is part of sex done well. It is true. Consent is also read. When the other's body changes, the right thing is to stop and ask, not to hope everything is fine.
- Looking after the afterwards, with affection, a conversation or a glass of water, matters, especially after intense practices. It is true. What happens afterwards is part of the experience. In intense practices, this care is agreed in advance.

### Nudes, screens and apps

What changes when sex goes through the phone.

- Sharing a nude you received, without permission, is a crime in many countries. It is true. Many countries now have specific laws against sharing intimate images without consent, often with heavier penalties for former partners.
- Whoever sent the nude accepted the risk: the leak is the sender's fault. It is a myth. Sending it to one person is trusting them, not authorising the world. The fault lies with whoever shared it.
- Recording sex without the other person knowing is a harmless keepsake. It is a myth. It is recording someone's intimacy without consent. It is a crime in many countries, even if the video is never shown to anyone.
- Asking insistently for nudes after a no is harassment. It is true. The same rule as in the physical world applies: after a no, insisting is pressure.
- Sexual montages and deepfakes with the faces of real people are a form of violence, even though they are fake. It is true. The harm to the person is real: exposure, humiliation and blackmail. Several countries already treat it as a crime.
- Using an artificial intelligence app to undress someone in a photo is harmless, as long as the image stays with you. It is a myth. It is creating a sexual image of a real person without their consent, and the violation lies in making it, not only in sharing it. Some countries already punish the creation itself.
- Keeping or sharing a sexual image of someone under 18 is a crime in most countries, even if the teenager sent it themselves. It is true. Most countries punish even simple possession. Whoever receives one must not pass it on: the right thing is to report it and delete it.
- Matching on a dating app means consenting to sex on the date. It is a myth. A match is interest in talking. Consent is given in person, at the time, and it may not come.
- Threatening to release intimate images to get something is a crime, and the way forward is to keep the evidence and report it. It is true. It is known as sextortion. Giving in tends to increase the demands; keeping the messages and going to the police is what protects you.

### When it is about other people

What you do when it is not about you: someone runs down your partner, someone is exposed, a friend crosses the line.

- When a friend runs down your partner's body or sex life and you keep quiet so as not to spoil the mood, you stayed neutral. It is a myth. Silence is usually read as agreement. You can disagree without a fight: a simple line, such as don't talk about her, or him, like that, already changes the conversation.
- When someone speaks badly of your partner, there are only two ways out: agree or fight. It is a myth. There is dialogue: asking what the person saw, disagreeing calmly and telling gossip from a warning. Loyalty does not require a fight, and it does not go with approving.
- When someone you trust warns you that your partner treats you badly, it is worth listening before jumping to their defence. It is true. People outside sometimes see what passion hides. Listening is not agreeing: it is checking. Stay or Go helps you weigh it.
- Showing friends the nude your partner sent you is a sign of trust between friends. It is a myth. The photo was entrusted to you, not to the group. Showing it breaks that trust and, in many countries, is a crime.
- When someone shows an intimate photo of another person, the right thing is not to look, not to pass it on and to say that this is not done. It is true. Whoever looks and laughs becomes the audience, and the audience is what gives a leak its value. Refusing is what breaks the chain.
- Laughing when a leaked nude arrives in the group chat harms nobody: the one in the wrong is whoever leaked it. It is a myth. Whoever leaked it was wrong first, but every laugh and every forward adds to the harm done to the person exposed.
- Telling someone that an intimate photo of them is circulating is helping, even though it is a hard conversation. It is true. The sooner the person knows, the sooner they can ask for removal, keep the evidence and report it. Tell them with care and without passing the image on.
- Seeing a friend insisting with someone who has drunk too much and doing nothing is respecting his life. It is a myth. It is letting violence happen. You can step in without confrontation: take the friend aside, ask the person whether they are all right, walk them to their friends or ask the venue staff for help.
- Calling out a friend who crossed the line with someone is betraying the friendship. It is a myth. It is the opposite: a friend is the one who says what others will not. Keeping quiet protects the wrong, not the friend.
- When someone tells you they suffered sexual violence, it helps to ask what they were wearing or why they went there. It is a myth. Those questions put the blame on the person who suffered. What helps is believing, listening without hurry and asking what they need.
- Spreading that someone is easy, has been around or is a virgin is harmless gossip. It is a myth. It is exposing someone's intimacy in order to diminish them. A person's sex life is not a public matter, whether it is a lot, a little or none.
- After a breakup, an ex's intimacy is still theirs: telling secrets or showing photos is still wrong. It is true. The end of the relationship does not cancel the trust with which those things were shared. Exposing an ex out of anger is one of the most common forms of leak.
- A joke about forcing someone is just humour and changes nothing. It is a myth. Jokes like that treat violence as a small thing. Research on sexist humour indicates that it raises tolerance of discrimination in those who are already prejudiced.

## The site's terms, and the ones outside it

- Property: What one feels for someone: a dimension of the bond, like Trust or Possession. The site has eighteen.
- Sub-property: A nameable component of a property. Trust has honesty, loyalty, competence, predictability, emotional and physical safety.
- Item: The concrete question that measures a sub-property on the scale.
- Value: The measure of what is felt, from 0 to 10, at that moment. Zero is a legitimate value.
- Weight: How much a property matters to you, separate from how much of it you feel. The difference between value and weight is one of the most revealing results.
- Variability: How much a value or a position swings over time. The word is variability, not inconsistency: inconsistency judges, variability describes.
- Profile: The set of one person's eighteen values for another.
- Portrait: A dated profile. The test always produces a portrait, never a truth; that's why it's worth redoing.
- Love type: A region of the portrait space: a recognizable pattern of high and low properties, like philia or storge. Never a goal.
- Modulator: What, in the one who feels, distorts the value: attachment, personality, trauma, moment, neediness, gender role.
- Shadow: A negative-sign property that is also part of the bond: hurt, rivalry, fear, contempt. On the radar, the gray layer.
- Root: Where a value comes from. The same value can have different roots: Possession 7 from fear of loss or from feeling like an owner.
- Expression trait: How a value shows on the outside. The same value comes out differently in an aggressive and in a peaceful person.
- Mechanism: The whole chain: root, property, expression trait, behavior. Only the behavior is what the other sees.
- Heuristic: The shortcut we use to predict whether it will work out: red flags and green flags.
- Constellation: The overlay of three or more people's portraits: what repeats among those you keep close is a portrait of you.
- Cut-off line: A Compatibility sub-property that is binary, not a scale: children, religion, where to live, what one eats.
- Availability thermometer: Five items before the scale that measure how open or closed to connection the person is right now. It doesn't alter the values; it alters the reading.
- Self map: The result of Self Discover: where you are on each slider, and where society presumes you.
- Presumed (the left-hand rule): On every slider, the leftmost position is what society presumes of someone until proven otherwise. Not the right one nor the common one: the presumed one.
- Equifinality: Different roots reach the same value. Possession 7 from fear and Possession 7 from property score the same.
- Multifinality: The same root produces different behaviors. The same fear of loss becomes a scene in an aggressive person and silent clinging in a peaceful one.
- Cross-cutting root: A root that distorts all values at once: the moment (closed to connection) and neediness (everything high).
- Sources of value: Where the image you form of someone comes from: direct perception, expectation, positive and negative discoveries, reputation, approval of the circle.
- Expectation (expected value): What you expected to feel or find before you knew the person. High expectation is the raw material of idealization.
- Discovery: What raised or lowered the value over time. The distance between expected and felt is the story of the bond told in discoveries.
- Reputation: What people say about the person. Weighs on Trust and Admiration before any evidence; the biggest source of borrowed flags.
- Approval of the circle: What friends and family say about the bond. Predicts duration better than common sense admits; the Romeo and Juliet effect did not hold up.
- Attraction: What pulls me toward the person: physical, charm, sexual, fetish, intellectual, chemistry, status, aesthetic.
- Passion: How much the person occupies my mental space: frequency of thought, euphoria, idealization, urgency, fascination, obsession.
- Admiration: What elevates me in the person: character, talent, achievements, style, courage, respect, pride, inspiration. You can love without admiring.
- Affection: The warmth: tenderness, care, missing them, comfort in their presence, non-sexual touch, compassion.
- Intimacy: How well we know each other: the stock of what is already known. Different from Openness, which is the channel open now.
- Openness: The channel between us, in both directions: outbound (emotional openness, what I show) and inbound (receptivity, what I take in).
- Emotional openness: The outbound side of the channel: how much of what I feel I say and show, including what I hide.
- Emotional receptivity: The inbound side of the channel: how willing I am to receive what the other feels, without defending or minimizing.
- Compatibility: How well our lives fit: values, practical life, intimate, daily life, project. Fit, not admiration.
- Trust: How safe I feel: honesty, loyalty, competence, predictability, emotional and physical safety.
- Support: What they do for me and I for them: emotional, practical, material, availability. Two directions, I give and I receive.
- Protection: I place myself between them and what threatens them. The shadow is overprotection, which turns into control.
- Investment: What I spend on them: time, money, energy, priority, opportunity cost, sacrifice.
- Commitment: The decision to stay: intention, plans, agreed exclusivity, resistance to alternatives, duty, habit.
- Possession: How much I want them to be mine: jealousy, desired exclusivity, control, fear of loss, comparison, territoriality.
- Dependence: How much I need them: emotional, practical, social, identity, fusion. Possession is I want to have you; dependence is I can't manage without you.
- Freedom: How much I remain myself inside the bond. The received side of the other's Possession; low, it is feeling trapped.
- Time: The shape of the bond over time: duration, frequency, rhythm, phase, projection, nostalgia, novelty, monotony.
- Reciprocity: What I think comes back: perception of being loved, balance of effort, gratitude, debt, known asymmetry.
- Shadows: What makes up the bond with a negative sign: hurt, rivalry, fear, anger, contempt, boredom, pity, shame.
- Novelty and monotony: How much is still new between us, and the routine that erases. It is what time does to Passion.
- Attachment: The way someone bonds and reacts to distance and loss. A trait of the one who feels, not a value of the bond.
- Secure attachment: Trusts, asks, lets go, comes back. Reads values closest to real.
- Anxious attachment: Fears abandonment; raises Possession, Dependence and Passion; marks threat where there is none.
- Avoidant attachment: Closes by default; lowers Openness, Intimacy and declared Dependence.
- Disorganized attachment: Wants and fears at the same time; swings between anxious and avoidant. Common after abuse.
- Big Five: The five major personality traits: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism.
- Neuroticism: The tendency to intense, swinging negative emotions. On the site, the Emotional reactivity slider.
- Neediness: Hunger for a bond: not lack of contact, lack of being cared for. Inflates Dependence, Passion, Investment and Possession; lowers standards.
- Loneliness: Lack of contact. Not neediness: you can be surrounded by people and needy, or alone and whole.
- Availability for connection: The state, not the trait: how open or closed the person is right now to letting someone in.
- Window of tolerance: The range in which a person can feel without shutting down or exploding (Siegel). Outside it, values come out distorted.
- Gender role: The script society assigns to each gender within the bond: who provides, cares, initiates, yields, protects, shows emotion.
- Aggressiveness and peacefulness: The main expression trait: the aggressive confronts, the peaceful goes quiet. Neither changes the value.
- Assertiveness: The healthy point between the two: I say what I feel, without attacking and without going silent.
- Property (root): Jealousy from feeling like an owner: fires at the other's autonomy, no rival needed; asks for obedience.
- Fear of loss: Jealousy from anticipating abandonment: fires at absence and any third party; asks for reassurance.
- Comparison: Jealousy from low self-worth: needs a concrete rival; asks to be chosen.
- Scarcity: Jealousy from fear of sharing time and attention: fires at friends, work, screens; asks for priority.
- Betrayal trauma: Hypervigilance to the exact trigger of an old betrayal, lived with someone else. Today's person pays for another.
- Projection: Attributing one's own impulse to the other: accusing them of straying because you want to stray.
- Cultural script: What culture teaches us to feel and to perform: jealousy as proof of love, for instance.
- Jealousy and envy: Jealousy is triangular (me, them, a third party) and fears losing what it has. Envy is a pair (me and whoever has what I want).
- Compersion: Feeling joy at a partner's joy with someone else. The inverse of jealousy.
- Sunk cost: Continuing because you've invested too much to leave (Rusbult). The most common reason to stay and the one least tied to love.
- Idealization: Seeing more than there is. Passion disguised as admiration; high expectation is the raw material.
- Limerence: The state of obsession with someone, with euphoria, withdrawal and idealization (Tennov). The shadow of Passion; lasts 12 to 30 months.
- Intermittence: Vanishing and coming back. Rekindles Passion through anxiety, not desire; addictive and erodes Trust. The toxic version of novelty.
- Intermittent reinforcement: The mechanism behind intermittence: unpredictable reward holds more than constant reward.
- Hedonic adaptation: The brain habituates to the predictable. That's why Passion falls.
- Self-expansion: Doing new things together sustains attraction (Aron). The ingredient is novelty, not pleasure.
- The four horsemen: Criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling: the four patterns that, for Gottman, best predict the end.
- Stonewalling: Shutting down and no longer responding during conflict. The peaceful expression of anger.
- Bids for attention: The small gestures that ask for a response through the day. Answering them is what, for Gottman, keeps the bond.
- Halo effect: Reading charm, beauty, status and intensity as signs of character. The most expensive false green in love.
- Red flag, green flag, beige flag: A sign of threat, a sign it tends to work out, and a sign that predicts nothing but is treated as if it did.
- False red: Trauma paints neutral things red. The flag is in the reader, not in the person.
- Love bombing: Enormous intensity in the first week: gifts, declarations, presence. High Passion with baseless Trust.
- Gaslighting: Making someone doubt their own memory and perception. A form of manipulation; a red line in Stay or Go.
- Emotional blackmail: Using guilt, fear or threat to get what one wants. Manipulation.
- Ghosting: Disappearing without explanation. Intermittence taken to the end.
- Breadcrumbing: Giving crumbs of attention to keep someone close without commitment. Intermittent reinforcement on purpose.
- Orbiting: Leaving someone's life but keeping watch from afar, usually through social media.
- Benching: Keeping someone on the bench: neither moving forward nor letting go, to keep the option.
- Trauma bonding: The bond that forms with someone who alternates abuse and affection. Explains why leaving is so hard.
- Codependency: Needing to be needed: organizing one's life around caring for someone who doesn't care for themselves. Two-way dependence.
- Social capital: What a person is worth in the eyes of others: prestige, circle, success, recognized beauty. And how much of it they lend to whoever is with them.
- Status: A person's place on the social ladder. A sub-property of Attraction and a root of Admiration; it weighs on almost everyone's attraction, to some degree.
- Hypergamy: The tendency to choose someone higher on the social ladder. Described as a human trait, not as anyone's flaw.
- Social proof: Finding someone attractive because others do. The value comes from the queue, not the person.
- Trophy partner: The person chosen in part for what they say about the one who chose them. High Bond in public with Admiration through pride in being seen.
- Borrowed importance: Feeling important for being with someone important. Usually comes with dependence on approval in Self Love.
- Eros: High Attraction and Passion. The love that pulls.
- Philia: Friendship: high Compatibility, Trust and Openness, Attraction near zero.
- Storge: Family love: Affection, Commitment and long time, often without admiration and without choice.
- Agape: High Support and Affection without expecting a return. The love that gives.
- Ludus: Attraction and light company, zero Commitment. Love as a game.
- Pragma: Commitment, Investment and Compatibility with low Passion. The love that chooses and builds.
- Mania: High Passion, Possession and Dependence. The love that consumes.
- Philautia: Self-love. The same ruler pointed inward: Self Love.
- Xenia: Hospitality: affection toward the stranger.
- Triangular theory: Intimacy, passion and commitment (Sternberg) generate eight types. The Love Theory is a higher-resolution version: eighteen properties.
- Consummate love: High Intimacy, Passion and Commitment at the same time. Rare and unstable; time moves one of the three.
- Companionate love: High Intimacy, Affection, Trust and Commitment with low Passion. The love of those who stayed.
- Infatuation: High Passion with no intimacy and no commitment. Limerence.
- Empty love: High Commitment with the rest low. One stays by decision, habit or duty.
- Parasocial love: Fan love: high Admiration, Passion and Investment, zero Reciprocity, imagined intimacy (Horton and Wohl).
- Platonic: Intimacy and Commitment without romantic or sexual attraction.
- Queerplatonic: A bond stronger and more committed than ordinary friendship, without being romantic. Born in the aromantic community.
- Residual love: What remains of an ex: high time and nostalgia, zero Commitment, shadows in between.
- Monogamy: Agreed and, in general, desired exclusivity.
- Monogamish: Not quite traditional monogamy: tends toward closed relationships, with some agreed flexibility. The term is Dan Savage's.
- Ethical non-monogamy: Any structure without exclusivity where everyone knows and agrees: open relationship, polyamory, relationship anarchy.
- Open relationship: A couple that admits other bonds, usually sexual, with agreed rules.
- Polyamory: More than one loving bond at the same time, with everyone's knowledge.
- Relationship anarchy: No prior hierarchy between bonds: each relationship defines its own rules.
- Metamour: Your partner's partner, with whom you have no direct bond.
- Polycule: The network of people linked by polyamorous bonds.
- NRE (new relationship energy): The euphoria at the start of a bond, named by the polyamorous community. Passion before time acts.
- Situationship: A bond with no name and no agreement: Commitment undefined by choice. The assumed layer tends to diverge.
- Friends with benefits: Friendship with sex and no agreed romantic commitment.
- Talking stage: The phase before the bond, when the two get to know each other with nothing agreed.
- Companion animal love: Very high Affection, Support and Trust, zero Attraction, one-sided Openness. Full love by the model.
- Sexual orientation: Which way sexual attraction points: hetero, homo, bi, pan, asexual and others.
- Romantic orientation: Which way romantic attraction points, separate from the sexual one: aromantic, biromantic and others.
- Split attraction model: The idea that sexual and romantic attraction are separate axes. Explains I love but don't desire and I desire but don't love.
- Bisexual: Attraction to more than one gender.
- Pansexual: Attraction in which gender is not a criterion. On the site, a marker apart from the slider, not a point on it.
- Omnisexual: Attraction to all genders, with gender still noticed. Close to pan.
- Asexual: Little or no sexual attraction. A spectrum, not a box.
- Gray-A: The gray zone of the asexual spectrum: rare or weak sexual attraction.
- Demisexual: Sexual attraction only after an emotional bond.
- Aromantic: Little or no romantic attraction. Aromantic people love friends, family, animals.
- Aroace: Aromantic and asexual.
- Types of attraction: Sexual, romantic, sensual, aesthetic, platonic, intellectual. They are the sub-properties of the Attraction family.
- Sapiosexual: Attraction above all to intelligence. The intellectual sub-property of Attraction as the main criterion.
- Libido: How much sexual desire the person feels, in general. Varies with time, health and phase; not a defect.
- Kink and fetish: Practices and preferences outside the common sexual script. Consensual, common, a sub-property of Attraction.
- Vanilla: The common sexual script, without kink. The presumed standard of the sexual openness slider.
- Gender identity: Which gender the person identifies with: cis, trans, non-binary, fluid. Not orientation and not expression.
- Cisgender: Someone who identifies with the gender assigned at birth.
- Transgender: Someone who identifies with a gender different from the one assigned at birth.
- Non-binary: Someone who doesn't identify only as a man or only as a woman: outside the two, or between them.
- Genderfluid: An identity that moves over time. On the site, the slider's variability, not a position.
- Gender expression: How the person presents: clothes, voice, gesture. Separate from identity and role.
- Kinsey scale: The 1948 scale from 0 (hetero) to 6 (homo). The site's orientation slider is that scale in five positions.
- Fisher's three systems: Lust, romantic attraction and attachment as separate brain circuits, which can point to different people at the same time.
- Love languages: Words, time, gifts, acts, touch (Chapman). Weak evidence as a theory; useful as a preference for giving and receiving.
- Red line: What does not enter the balance: violence, threats, coercion, betrayal, compulsive lying, manipulation, control, humiliation. Reasons in themselves.
- Balance: Pros and cons, each with a score and a weight, as a percentage on each side. Never a verdict.
- Score and weight: The score is what you feel; the weight is how much it matters to you. The balance recalculates when the weight changes.
- Reasons of love: Love, affection and history, growing together.
- Reasons of prison: Habit, fear of being alone, duty, money, sunk cost, hope of change, fear of what people will say, not knowing who I would be.
- Reasons of responsibility: Children. Legitimate, and neither love nor prison.
- Repair: What happens after the break: naming, acknowledging, changing. A single betrayal only resolves with real repair, accepted by both.
- Sexual coercion: Pressuring, insisting after a no, treating sex as an obligation. A red line from the first time.
- Coercive control: Controlling money, phone, clothes, whom one talks to; isolating from friends and family. A red line.
- Manipulation: Making the other doubt themselves, emotional blackmail, guilt as a weapon. A red line.
- Sex education: What one knows, from reliable sources, about the body, pleasure, consent, contraception and sexually transmitted infections. An extra slider in Self Discover: it does not measure experience.
- Consent: The free, informed and specific yes, given beforehand and withdrawable at any moment. A yes given to please or after insistence is not consent.
- Safe word: The word agreed beforehand that stops any practice at once, with no discussion. Indispensable in power play.
- Yes, no, maybe list: Each person marks alone what they want, do not want and might want; the match shows only what coincides. It is the format of Keep the Spark and the Sexual Bucketlist.
- Bucket list: The list of what one wants to live. The site has two: the love one and the sexual one.
- Swinging: Partner swapping. In a soft swap it stays at kissing and touching; a full swap includes sex. Always with the agreement of all four.
- Threesome: Sex among three people. It only works when all three want it and the couple agreed beforehand what is and is not allowed.
- Hall pass: The agreed permission to be with someone else on a defined occasion, while the relationship stays exclusive the rest of the time.
- Voyeurism and exhibitionism: The pleasure of watching and the pleasure of being watched. Between consenting adults it is a preference; with someone who did not consent it is a violation.
- Pegging: Role reversal in penetration: the one who is usually penetrated penetrates their partner, with a strap-on or a toy.
- Edging: Getting close to orgasm and backing off, several times, to prolong and intensify it.
- Shared novelty: What routine wears out and Passion asks for. In Aron's experiments (2000), couples who did new and exciting activities together reported better relationship quality; the self-expansion model proposes that this counters boredom.
- Unwanted sexual touching: Performing a sexual act on someone without their consent, such as groping or rubbing against them. A crime in many countries.
- Sexual coercion: Getting sex through insistence, blackmail, threat or guilt. There is no physical force, and still the yes is not free.
- Stealthing: Secretly removing the condom during sex. It violates consent, which was for protected sex.
- Arousal non-concordance: The body can respond (erection, lubrication) without the person desiring or consenting. A body response is not consent.
- Orgasm gap: In sex between a man and a woman, women have orgasms less often than men. Studies point to the script centred on penetration, not the body.
- Responsive desire: Desire that appears after stimulation instead of out of nowhere. As normal as spontaneous desire.
- Undetectable = untransmittable: Someone living with HIV who is on treatment and keeps an undetectable viral load does not transmit the virus through sex.
- PrEP and PEP: Medicines that prevent HIV infection: PrEP is taken before exposure; PEP, after, within 72 hours.
- Objectification: Treating a person as a thing: seeing the body and ignoring the will, the pleasure and the feelings. Desiring someone's body is not objectifying; reducing the person to it is.
- Emotional responsibility: Being honest about what you want and caring about the effect of your choices on whoever is with you, in casual sex too.
